name: .sg2 / .sg3 + .555
title: The SG asset pipeline
note: Documented. An .sg2/.sg3 index over pixel data held in sibling .555 files — the shared art pipeline for the whole isometric era.
summary: Every sprite in Caesar III, Pharaoh, Zeus and Emperor comes through this pair of files: an .sg2 or .sg3 index describing images, and one or more .555 files holding their pixels. Getting art out of these games, or new art in, means reading both.

body: An SG file contains no pixels. It is an index: a fixed header, a lookup table, one record per source bitmap, and one record per image. The pixels live in .555 files, and every image record points into one by byte offset.

The split is what makes the format tractable. You can read the whole catalogue of a game's art — names, dimensions, animation frames, which building a sprite belongs to — without decoding a single pixel.

rows.description: Maps a stable game-facing group ID to the position of an image record. The indirection is the point: artists could reorder or re-export images without the game code having to change.

spec.note: 200 bytes each, following the index. One per source bitmap — the artist's original file, which may hold many game images.

spec.title: Image types
spec.note: Read from offset 50 of an image record.

items.description: Plain image that may carry transparency.
Plain images.
Isometric — a building or terrain tile, stored differently. See below.

spec.title: How pixels are stored
body: Three storage modes, chosen per image by the flags at offsets 51 to 53.
Uncompressed images are raw pixels, row by row, top to bottom and left to right.

Compressed images are run-length encoded, and only for transparency. A control byte of 255 means "the next byte is a count of transparent pixels"; any other value is a count of coloured pixels that follow. There is no compression of the colours themselves.

Isometric images come in two parts. The base is a set of uncompressed diamond tiles — 58×30 pixels in Caesar III, Pharaoh and Zeus, and 78×40 in Emperor — laid out row by row for multi-tile buildings. Anything standing above the ground plane follows as a compressed "top" section.

spec.title: The .555 files and colour
body: Pixels are two bytes each, little-endian, five bits per channel in R-G-B order. The single value 0xF81F is the transparency key rather than a colour, which is why it never appears as magenta in-game.

Most images live in the internal .555 file, which shares the SG file's name. Some live in external ones, flagged at offset 52 of the image record and named after the bitmap record's filename with the extension changed to .555. Pharaoh in particular spreads its art across several external files.

spec.title: A useful sanity check
spec.body: A frequently reported figure for the fixed prelude of an SG file is 20,680 bytes. That is not a magic number: it is 80 bytes of header, plus the 600-byte index, plus 100 bitmap records of 200 bytes each. If a file you are parsing does not agree, read the bitmap record count at offset 20 rather than assuming 100.

name: .eng
title: The ENG text format
note: Documented. Holds every string in the game, plus the layout of the message dialogs — the file any translation has to go through.
summary: All of a game's text lives in .eng files: one for strings, one ending _mm.eng for the pop-up messages, which carries dialog geometry alongside the words. Anyone translating one of these games, or reading its text out, works here.

body: Two related files, both in three parts: a short header, a fixed-size index, and a data section of null-separated strings.

The wiki documents Caesar III as its worked example — its files identify themselves with a descriptor string like "C3 textfile." — and the later titles use the same structure with their own descriptor and their own quirks.

spec.title: Text file header
spec.note: 28 bytes.

rows.name: descriptor
rows.description: Identifies the file and the game, e.g. "C3 textfile."

rows.name: num_groups
rows.description: Highest group ID in use, plus one.

rows.name: num_strings
rows.description: Total strings in the file.

rows.name: num_words
rows.description: Word count. Not reliable — do not use it to size a buffer.

spec.title: Text file index
spec.note: 1,000 entries of 8 bytes each, following the header.

rows.name: offset
rows.description: Where this group's strings begin in the data section.

rows.name: in_use
rows.description: In the earlier games a flag, 0 or 1. In the later ones, the number of strings in the group.

spec.title: Text data and encoding
body: Strings run consecutively, separated by null bytes, and a string must contain at least one printable character — a byte of 32 or above — to count.

There is no encoding declared anywhere in the file; it follows from the language of the release. Western European editions use Windows-1252, Polish uses Windows-1250, Russian Windows-1251, and Korean Windows-950. Traditional Chinese uses an encoding of its own.

spec.title: Message file header
spec.note: 24 bytes. Message files are the ones whose names end in _mm.eng.

rows.name: descriptor
rows.description: Identifies the file, e.g. "C3 MMfile".

rows.name: num_entries
rows.description: Index entries present — typically 1,000.

rows.name: num_used
rows.description: Highest index in use, plus one.

spec.title: Message index entry
spec.note: 80 bytes each. This is where the format stops being a string table: each entry lays out the dialog the message appears in.

spec.title: Not fully documented
spec.body: The wiki's tables for message types and subtypes are marked TODO, and several positioning fields between offsets 34 and 55 have no established meaning. A parser can read every message and lay out every dialog without them; a tool that wants to create new messages cannot.

name: .map
title: The Caesar III scenario format
note: Structure confirmed: ten uncompressed chunks in a fixed order, 211,692 bytes exactly. The scenario block's own internals are not documented.
summary: A Caesar III scenario is not a container with a table of contents. It is ten fixed-size blocks written back to back in a known order, none of them compressed — which makes it the easiest file in the whole series to take apart.

body: Nobody has published a specification for this format. What exists is Julius's reimplementation, which reads and writes the original files exactly, so its loader is the closest thing to one. Everything below is read off that code rather than inferred from files.
The whole scenario is ten chunks in a fixed order with no headers, no lengths and no markers between them. Every chunk is uncompressed — unlike a savegame, where most are not.

spec.title: Chunks, in order
spec.note: Sizes in bytes. Offsets are cumulative and implied by the order, since nothing in the file records them.

rows.name: graphic_ids
rows.description: Two bytes per tile.

rows.name: edge
rows.description: One byte per tile.

rows.name: terrain
rows.description: Two bytes per tile.

rows.name: bitfields
rows.description: One byte per tile.

rows.name: random
rows.description: One byte per tile.

rows.name: elevation
rows.description: One byte per tile.

rows.name: random_iv
rows.description: Seed state for the random number generator.

rows.name: camera
rows.description: Saved camera position.

rows.name: scenario
rows.description: The scenario proper: name, briefing, victory conditions, invasions, requests, prices. Its internal layout is not documented here.

rows.name: end_marker
rows.description: Closes the file.

spec.title: The map is always 162 × 162
spec.body: Every per-tile chunk is either 26,244 bytes or twice that, and 26,244 is 162 squared — Julius defines GRID_SIZE as 162. The playable area is smaller; the grid includes an unusable border. This also means the total file size is fixed at 211,692 bytes, which is the quickest way to tell a genuine Caesar III scenario from something else.

spec.title: Later titles are a different problem
spec.body: This describes Caesar III only. Pharaoh, Zeus and Emperor have their own scenario formats, and Julius does not read them. Akhenaten and the Ozymandias projects are the nearest equivalent for Pharaoh; nobody has written any of them up.

name: .sav
title: The Caesar III savegame format
note: Container structure confirmed from Julius: an ordered chunk list, most chunks compressed with PKWARE DCL. What is inside most chunks is not documented.
summary: A savegame is the scenario format's larger sibling: the same idea of ordered chunks with nothing to separate them, but many more of them and most compressed. The container is well understood; the contents mostly are not.

body: As with scenarios, there is no published specification and Julius's loader is the reference. It reads a savegame as an ordered list of up to a hundred chunks, of which it names seventy-two.
The difference from a scenario is compression. Each chunk carries a flag saying whether it is stored compressed, and the compressed ones are framed.

spec.title: A compressed chunk
spec.note: Uncompressed chunks have no framing at all — the raw bytes simply follow, and you must already know how many.

rows.name: length
rows.description: Length of the compressed data that follows — or the sentinel 0x80000000, meaning compression was not worth it and the raw data follows instead.

rows.name: data
rows.description: Compressed, or raw when the sentinel is present.

spec.title: It is not ZIP, despite the function names
spec.body: Julius calls these zip_compress and zip_decompress, and the file is core/zip.c — but the implementation is pk_implode and pk_explode, the PKWARE Data Compression Library. That is a different algorithm from DEFLATE, so a zlib call on this data will fail. The naming has misled people; the lookup tables and the 516-byte maximum match length are what settle it.

items.description: The save version Julius writes.
Chunk sentinel meaning the data that follows is uncompressed.
Julius's compression buffer size — an upper bound on a single chunk, not a format constant.
Size of the end marker: seventy-one four-byte zeroes.

spec.title: What is missing
spec.body: Knowing the chunk order and how to decompress each one gets you seventy-two byte arrays. Julius names them, so you know which holds buildings and which holds figures, but the record layout inside each is only described by the code that consumes it. Anyone wanting a save editor has to read that code. This is the largest genuinely open documentation gap in the Caesar III lineage.

name: c3_model.txt
title: The c3_model.txt balance file
note: Documented. The plain-text file holding every building's cost and labour requirement — the one modders edit to rebalance the game.
summary: Caesar III keeps none of its balance numbers in the executable. Building costs, labour requirements, desirability and the whole housing evolution ladder live in a plain-text file the game reads at startup, which is why rebalancing the game needs no patching at all.

body: c3_model.txt ships with the game and sits beside the executable. It is plain text, editable in any editor, and the engine parses it on startup — so changing a building's cost is a text edit rather than a patch. This is the single most useful file in the game for anyone who wants to rebalance it.

The parser is forgiving about layout and strict about counts. It looks for two section markers, then reads brace-delimited groups of comma-separated integers, skipping anything that is not a digit. Whitespace and formatting between values do not matter; the number of entries does.

spec.title: Sections
spec.note: Found by literal string match, in this order.

items.description: Followed by exactly 130 brace-delimited entries of 8 values each.
Followed by exactly 20 brace-delimited entries of 20 values each — the housing evolution ladder, one entry per level from small tent to luxury palace.

spec.title: A building entry
spec.note: Eight comma-separated integers. Position is the only key — nothing in the file is named.

rows.name: cost
rows.description: Cost to build. For walls and other draggable structures this is the cost of one tile.

rows.name: desirability_value
rows.description: Desirability contributed at the building's own tiles.

rows.name: desirability_step
rows.description: How far, in tiles, before the value steps.

rows.name: desirability_step_size
rows.description: How much the value changes at each step.

rows.name: desirability_range
rows.description: Maximum distance the effect reaches.

rows.name: laborers
rows.description: How many people the building employs.
Read and discarded by Julius.

spec.title: House entries
body: Twenty values each, and between them they define the entire housing ladder: the desirability needed to evolve and the level at which a house devolves, then the requirements a house must have met — entertainment, water, religion, education, barber, bathhouse, health, how many food types, pottery, oil, furniture and wine — followed by prosperity, the maximum population of the level, and a tax multiplier.
That list is the whole of Caesar III's housing model, in twenty numbers per level. Nothing else in the game decides whether an insula becomes a villa.

spec.title: It fails loudly, which is a gift
spec.body: Julius counts what it parsed and refuses to start unless it found exactly 150 entries — 130 buildings and 20 houses. An edited file that drops or gains a brace does not produce a subtly wrong game; it produces a refusal to load. When editing, keep the counts and change only the numbers.

spec.title: Why this site does not publish the values
spec.body: The numbers in this file are per-installation. They differ between game versions and any mod may rewrite them, so a table of costs frozen here would be right for one copy of the game and quietly wrong for others. The file is on the reader's own disk, it is plain text, and now they know what each column means — which is more durable than a copy of one version's numbers.

name: .map / .sav
note: Undocumented. These titles have their own scenario and save formats, and no public write-up exists — Akhenaten and the Ozymandias projects are the closest thing to a spec for Pharaoh.

name: .VPX
title: The Caesar .VPX picture format
note: Full-screen 320×200 pictures: four run-length-coded blocks, interleaved a byte at a time, with no palette inside. Decoded and matched against the running game.
summary: Every full-screen picture in Caesar — the title, the Forum, the battle, the map of the Empire — is a .VPX file: four blocks of run-length-coded bytes that interleave into a 320 × 200 image of palette indices. The file carries no colours. The game loads a palette from a separate file before it shows each picture, and which palette goes with which picture is the part that has to be looked up.

spec.title: Layout
body: A .VPX file is exactly four blocks back to back, with nothing before, between or after them. Each block is an 8-byte header followed by its compressed payload, and each decodes to exactly 16,000 bytes: a quarter of the picture. A file whose blocks do not end exactly where the file ends is malformed, and the decoder here rejects it rather than guessing.
There are twenty in the US build. All decode to 320 × 200, one byte per pixel.

spec.title: Block header, 8 bytes, once per block

rows.name: packed_size
rows.description: Size of the whole block in bytes, this header included. The next block starts that far on.

rows.name: decoded_size
rows.description: Always 16000 (0x3E80) in every shipped file.

rows.name: fill A
rows.description: The low byte of the header's third word: the byte a "fill A" command repeats.

rows.name: fill B
rows.description: The high byte: the byte a "fill B" command repeats.

rows.name: field3
rows.description: Read by the engine, not needed to decode. Purpose not established.

rows.name: payload
rows.description: The command stream, read until the block has produced 16,000 bytes.

spec.title: Commands
spec.note: n is the low six bits of the command byte, so every run is 1 to 64 bytes long.

items.description: Explicit run: repeat the byte that follows, n + 1 times.
Fill A run: repeat the header's fill A byte n + 1 times.
Fill B run: repeat the header's fill B byte n + 1 times.
Literal run: copy the next n + 1 bytes unchanged.

spec.title: Putting the planes together
body: The four decoded blocks are not bit planes. They interleave one byte at a time: byte i of plane p (p from 0 to 3) is pixel 4i + p of the picture, read row by row. That is the memory layout of VGA's unchained 256-colour mode, where each plane holds every fourth column; the engine copies a block to the screen one plane at a time. The explanation is an inference from the sprite sheets, where the executable's blitter was read directly; the interleave itself is not.
The same layout is used by the .PL8 sprite sheets and the .VAS animations.

spec.title: Which palette goes with which picture
spec.note: Twenty pictures. "Definitive" means the engine's own load was read or a capture of the real screen matches; the rest are matched by eye.

items.description: EMAP2.P32. Definitive: matches a capture of the map screen on 63,144 of 64,000 pixels, every difference being the province markers and status text the game draws on top.
NEWFORUM.256. Definitive: the Forum capture's palette equals it in all 256 entries.
TEMPLE.256. Definitive: loaded with it by the ratings screen.
WAR2.256. Definitive: the battle screen, and the offer to hand a battle to the separate Cohort 2 program.
SHADE.256, the interface palette. Definitive: the governor's page.
PANEL1.256, or PANEL1.P32: the two agree on every index the picture uses.
TITLE3.256. Renders the title screen correctly.
LOSEPIC.P32 and WINPIC.P32 respectively. By name.
IMPRLOGO.256. By name for the first; inference for the second, the same intro sequence.
IMPRLOGO.256. Inference: the picture uses only the 16 standard VGA colours and one grey, which that palette holds.
ROME1.256. The natural-looking match; an inference for ROME2, which shows the same scene.
SHADE.256. Inference: the picture uses only colours 0 to 15, which SHADE, PANEL1 and TEMPLE share.
Unresolved. They use high palette indices that PANEL1.256 does not hold, and no palette has been matched to them.

spec.title: What this can't tell you
spec.body: The meaning of the header's fourth word. The palette for PANEL1A to PANEL1D. And the palette for four others (LOGO, ROME, IMPRSEN, ROME2) is a best match, not a read of the code that loads them. Everything above is the US build; the international build ships some pictures under other names (FORUM32.VPX, IMP_LOGO.VPX, WAR.VPX), which have not been analysed.

name: .PL8 / .PL1
title: The Caesar .PL8 sprite sheet format
note: Sprite and font sheets: a descriptor table, then pixels stored as four interleaved streams. Frames match the real city view pixel for pixel; the first header word is still unexplained.
summary: The city's tiles and buildings, its walkers, the toolbar's icons and every font are .PL8 sheets: a small table of frame descriptors followed by the frames' pixels. The descriptors are plain; the pixels are the part that took a capture of the running game to get right, because they are four interleaved streams rather than rows.

spec.title: Layout
body: A sheet starts with a four-byte container header and a table of frame descriptors, one per frame. A descriptor does not hold pixels, only where they are: the pixel data of every frame lives at an absolute offset in the same file. Frames are packed back to back.

rows.name: unknown_a
rows.description: 42 in HOUSES.PL8, 61 in the international build's MINIFONT.PL8. Not the frame count. Meaning not established.

rows.name: frame_count
rows.description: The number of descriptors that follow. Confirmed exactly against HOUSES.PL8's 50 frames.

rows.name: frames
rows.description: The descriptor table, starting immediately after the header.

rows.name: pixel_offset
rows.description: Absolute file offset of this frame's pixels. The one big-endian value in the format; everything else is little-endian.

rows.name: width
rows.description: In pixels. Always a multiple of 4 for a frame that has pixels.

rows.name: height
rows.description: In pixels.

rows.name: x
rows.description: The frame's origin x within its sheet's layout.

rows.name: y
rows.description: The frame's origin y.

spec.title: Pixels
body: A frame's width × height bytes are four streams stored one after another, interleaved one pixel at a time exactly as in a .VPX picture: pixel i, counted row by row, is entry i / 4 of stream i mod 4. The four streams are the planes of unchained VGA, each holding every fourth column, which is why a frame's width has to divide by four. Read row by row, no frame of the city view matches a capture of the real game; read this way, 13 HOUSES, 13 HOUSES2 and 72 FIXTS frames appear in the captures byte for byte, on the 16-pixel tile grid.

Colour index 0 is transparent when the engine draws a sprite. The ground tiles (every tile below 0xC8, from FIXTS.PL8) are drawn opaque. A frame's pixels are indices; the city sheets use only indices 0 to 15 of SHADE.256, the city palette.

spec.title: .PL1, the one-bit variant
body: MINIFONT.PL1 has the same container and descriptors, but one bit per pixel: each row is ceil(width / 8) bytes, most significant bit first, a set bit becoming pixel value 1 and a clear bit 0. The extension names the depth. The international build's 4,036-byte MINIFONT.PL8 is the same 72 frames at eight bits.

spec.title: The sheets, and what draws from them
spec.note: Frame counts are the US build's.

items.description: Terrain and every city tile below 0xC8, one frame per tile id (16 × 16). Drawn opaque.

Buildings and houses, tile 0xC8 and up. Its last six descriptors (frames 44 to 49) point at the end of the file and declare a size that would overrun it: empty placeholders. Why they exist is not explained.
Building states and animation frames, some of them 64 × 64.
Walkers and other city actors, drawn between the tile rows.
The province view's tiles and sprites. Strong inference: they load in place of the city sheets when the province is shown, and FIXT3 frames turn up in the map captures.
The battle screen's banners.
Frame, border and button pieces of the advisor and management screens: 31 of the 40 are found in captures.
The toolbar buttons' icons (each button record names its frame and its handler), the histories' bar pieces, and the province markers on the empire map.
The main text font; the engine picks a frame through a character table. FONT2.PL8 has the same shape and is the battle screen's font.
A second font: letters with case folded to frames 0 to 25 and a 27th frame for everything else.
Small capitals and digits: the histories' captions among other things.
The ratings screen's column pieces: the base, the shaft and the capital.
The shading frames the city view's overlay map modes draw, chosen from the land value, water and similar layers.

spec.title: What this can't tell you
spec.body: What the first header word means. Why HOUSES.PL8 ends in six placeholder frames. Which frame is which in most sheets: the city sheets are mapped to tile ids, but HOUSES2.PL8 and FIXT3.PL8 are only partly mapped, and several fonts were checked less than FONT1. The palette for the toolbar icons is the city palette; no sheet carries its own.

name: .256 / .P32
title: The Caesar palette formats, .256 and .P32
note: Two palette files: a raw 768-byte VGA DAC block, and a 32-colour packed version. Both checked against the DAC of the running game, entry by entry.
summary: Caesar's pictures and sprites are all indices; the colours live in eight .256 files and six .P32 files. The .256 file is nothing but the VGA palette registers' contents, and the executable hands it to the BIOS untouched. The only subtle thing about either format is how the six-bit values are widened to eight, which is a convention of whoever draws the picture rather than anything in the file.

spec.title: .256: a whole VGA palette
spec.note: In the executable the generic file loader reads the whole file into a buffer, and the palette routine passes that buffer untouched to the BIOS (INT 10h, function 1012h: set a block of DAC registers, 256 of them). So the file is the DAC block. In a non-VGA video mode the same routine programs only entries 0 to 15.

rows.name: colours
rows.description: Red, green, blue for each of 256 entries, each channel a six-bit VGA DAC value from 0 to 63. No header and no transform.

spec.title: .P32: thirty-two colours
spec.note: Each nibble n is a DAC value of n × 4, so 15 means 60, not 63. That comes from captures of the running game: the map and Forum screens hold EMAP2.P32 and FORUM32.P32 in the DAC as exactly n × 4, in all 32 entries each.

rows.name: colours
rows.description: Little-endian words, one per colour. Bits 0 to 3 are red, bits 8 to 11 are blue, bits 12 to 15 are green; bits 4 to 7 are unused. Note that green sits in the high nibble, above blue.

spec.title: Widening to eight bits
body: A DAC value is six bits (0 to 63). To show one on an eight-bit display, screenshot tools disagree: some write v << 2, some (v << 2) | (v >> 4). The game never does either, so a comparison with a capture should be made at six bits. The tools here use the second form.

spec.title: Which file is which
spec.note: All eight US-build .256 files are 768 bytes with every byte in 0 to 63; a byte above 63 is rejected.

items.description: The city palette, and the interface palette. All 256 entries equal the DAC of every city-view capture. SHADE.P32 is its first 20 entries.
The Forum. All 256 entries equal the Forum capture's DAC.
The battle screen, the ratings screen, the title screen, the ROME1 and ROME2 pictures, and the intro pictures.
The bottom panel. The first 32 entries of the .256 are exactly the .P32's nibbles times 4, and the picture renders to the same DAC value at all 64,000 pixels through either.
The map of the Empire, the Forum's 32 colours, and the two end-of-game pictures.

spec.title: What this can't tell you
spec.body: Which palette a given picture takes is not in either file. That table is on the .VPX page, with how sure each pairing is. The international build's palette files (it ships TEMPLE.P32, TITLE3.P32 and others) are not analysed here.

name: EMPIRE2.0NN
title: The Caesar province map format, EMPIRE2.0NN
note: Fifty files of exactly 1,602 bytes: a two-byte prefix and a 40 × 40 grid of tile bytes, one file per province. The layout is certain; the full vocabulary of tile values is not.
summary: Each of Caesar's fifty provinces is one EMPIRE2 file: the map the province view draws, the coast, the rivers, the towns and the borders where barbarians arrive. A saved game embeds a copy of the current one. The file is trivially simple. What the bytes in it mean is the part still being worked out.

spec.title: The whole file, 1,602 bytes
spec.note: All fifty files round-trip through load and save byte for byte.

rows.name: prefix
rows.description: 14 14 in all fifty files and in every save's embedded copy. The engine never reads it as a field: it is loaded and saved along with the map and is reached only by reads that run off the grid's top-left corner. It is not a width or height; the engine's 40s are constants.

rows.name: cells
rows.description: The map, row by row: the cell at row r, column c is byte 2 + 40r + c. One tile id per cell.

spec.title: Which province is which
body: The file for province NN is named EMPIRE2.0NN: the engine writes the province number as three decimal digits into the name and loads that. So EMPIRE2.000 is the first province and EMPIRE2.049 the last. A promotion that sends the governor to a new province loads the next one into the game state.

spec.title: Tile values the engine treats specially
spec.note: Most names are STRONG INFERENCE, matched by what the engine's own commands write and read rather than by a label in the file. The ranges for open ground and the cost shift are definitive.

items.description: Static terrain: water, mountains and the like. Never simulated; in real saves they form fixed blobs that are byte-identical from save to save.

Open ground. This is the only terrain the province's build commands will lay on; anything below 0x1D is refused. Within it, the cost of a province build is shifted left by the ground: twice (×4) on 0x25 to 0x2C, once (×2) on 0x2D to 0x35. That is the manual's "from 30 Denarii to 120 Denarii, depending on the terrain".
Provincial road, in twelve shapes (straight, corners, junctions). The same twelve as the city's road pieces.

The Imperial Highway's entry. When a province starts, the first 0x41 found scanning row by row becomes 0x78 and its position is remembered. This is the "unexplained" byte change between a raw scenario and the copy in a save.
Great Wall pieces, with 0x44 and 0x45 the gates where a road crosses a wall, and 0x62 to 0x67 the Great Towers. Names are a strong inference from what the wall command writes.
The capital city. The player's first Cohort is placed on the first cell holding 0x4A.
Towns, in order of size: 0x61 smallest, 0x4C largest.
A fort.
Where barbarian armies enter: from the sea (0x51 plus a race index) and by land (0x59 plus the same). 0x59 to 0x60 are also the land border markers.
Imperial Highway, in the same twelve shapes as the road. 0x7B and 0x7C are a road crossing a highway.
Not terrain: the engine sets it on the cells of a trace it is following. In the saves it is set on the capital's cell (0x4A becomes 0xCA).

spec.title: The fifty provinces, in file order
spec.note: The names are the executable's own, in a table of 16-character fields; "Caeariensis" is spelled so there. Each province is attacked by one of sixteen barbarian races, which the executable also tabulates.

spec.title: What this can't tell you
spec.body: The full vocabulary of tile values: the ranges above are the ones the code tests, and the rest are inferred. The 0x41 to 0x78 change was seen in one scenario of one session across all the saves, though the code that does it is read. How the cells were authored, and whether any scenario carries anything the engine ignores, is unknown beyond the prefix.

name: .SAV
title: The Caesar savegame format
note: Exactly 57,126 bytes in twenty fixed blocks: the game's globals, the walkers, the five city layers, the province map and the yearly histories. Every block is located; a few fields in them are not yet named.
summary: A Caesar save is a straight dump of the game's data segment, in the writer's order: 128 global words, the actor table, the city's five 100 × 100 layers and the rest. Nothing is compressed or indexed. The blocks' positions and sizes are certain, because the loader reads exactly what the writer writes; what is still partial is the meaning of some words and of the middle of an actor record.

spec.title: Layout
body: A save is 57,126 bytes (0xDF26), always. The game's writer makes 175 write calls, one per record, from the data segment straight to the file; its loader reads the same 175 records, at the same addresses and sizes, in the same order. So reading and writing are the same list, and Gaius's writer produces a file that is byte-identical to every one of seventeen real saves it was given.
Saves are named CAESARxx.SAV, with xx chosen by the player. Everything is little-endian.

spec.title: The twenty blocks, in file order
spec.note: Offsets and sizes in bytes. The block boundaries are confirmed by the loader, and by the footprint of every building in real saves coming out as an exact rectangle.

rows.name: global words
rows.description: The game's state words. They are not a contiguous run of addresses: the writer takes them in its own order (with 15 discontinuities, skipping one address and writing another twice). The funds are the word at 0x3E.

rows.name: actors
rows.description: The walker and army table: 70 records of 50 bytes. See the record below.

rows.name: Forums
rows.description: 16 bytes each: +0 column, +2 row, +4 grade (0 to 7), +6 timer, +8 active, +A a facing counter. The count of forums is capped at 30.

rows.name: Barracks
rows.description: 12 bytes each: +0 column, +2 row, +4 timer, +6 active, +8 facing.

rows.name: Workshops
rows.description: 24 bytes each: +0 column, +2 row, +4 goods type (0 to 7), +6 timer, +8 active, +A facing, +C population nearby, +E sales, +0x10 production level, +0x12 last level, +0x14 industry.

rows.name: tiles
rows.description: The city map: one tile id per cell, row by row (index = row × 100 + column). Ids below 0xC8 are terrain, roads, walls and water; 0xC8 to 0xD7 are the sixteen house grades.

rows.name: service flags
rows.description: Bit flags per cell: water (0x01), forum road access (0x02, a strong inference), bath houses (0x04), market (0x08), administration (0x20), school or hospital (0x40), entertainment (0x80). Rebuilt from the tiles at the end of every month.

rows.name: land value
rows.description: The Maps panel's "land value" layer, a signed byte per cell, built each month by every service building's reach.

rows.name: part index and state
rows.description: Low nibble: the cell's position inside its building, 4 × row offset + column offset, with 0 the anchor. Held by every cell of every multi-cell building in every save. Other bits are state flags, only partly understood.

rows.name: unrest
rows.description: The Maps panel's "trouble areas" layer, drawn on houses: a signed byte per cell, raised by what makes citizens unhappy and lowered by temples, prefectures, barracks and oracles. A low-grade house collapses when its cell exceeds a limit.

rows.name: province map
rows.description: The current province's map file, with game state written into it. See EMPIRE2.

rows.name: provinces given
rows.description: One flag per province already assigned to this governor.

rows.name: workshops per goods
rows.description: How many workshops of each of the eight goods are built.

rows.name: population milestones
rows.description: Flags for 200, 1000, 2000, 4000, 8000, 12000, 16000 and 20000 people having been reached. The last two bytes are unused.

rows.name: yearly histories
rows.description: Four tables of 15 (year, value) word pairs: population tax, industrial tax, funds, and population units.

rows.name: profit history
rows.description: The yearly profit or loss; 17 of the 18 records are used.

rows.name: final state
rows.description: Thirty-four more words (twelve of those bytes are the governor's name, padded with spaces to 12 characters; "  Octavian  " in every save), including the difficulty, the industrial tax rate, the monthly scan counters and last year's Treasurer's report.

spec.title: An actor record, 50 bytes
spec.note: The other bytes belong to movement, targets and timers. They are laid out in Gaius's source (systems/actors.hpp) but not tabulated here.

rows.name: frame
rows.description: The sprite frame drawn: from MOREMEN.PL8 in the city view, SPRITE2.PL8 in the province view.

rows.name: x
rows.description: World x in pixels. The sprite's bottom edge is drawn at y + 8.

rows.name: y
rows.description: World y in pixels.

rows.name: active
rows.description: Non-zero for a live record. The exact bit packing is not established.

rows.name: type
rows.description: The actor class, indexing a table of fourteen handlers: 0 to 10 are city walkers (forum citizens, workshop traders, barracks patrols, rioters, invaders), 11 a barbarian army, 12 an army arriving by sea, 13 a Cohort.

rows.name: index
rows.description: The record's own slot number; it matches the slot in every active record in the saves.

rows.name: destination or cell
rows.description: For a province actor, its current cell (column, row). For a city actor, where it is heading, not where it is.

rows.name: position
rows.description: For a city actor, row × 100 + column: the reliable position. For a province actor, row × 40 + column.

rows.name: state
rows.description: The behaviour: an index into a second table of sixteen handlers.

spec.title: Words worth knowing
spec.note: A few of the 162 words. Every one the writer saves has been identified by what reads and writes it; two (at data-segment addresses 0x6BDC and 0x6CBC) are never used.

items.description: The treasury, in denarii, at the global word at file offset 0x3E. Across a real session it falls 7182, 4692, 3210, 3144, which is how the word was pinned.
The month runs 0 to 11. The year is a signed counter, not a BC or AD date: a new game starts at −13, and one session's saves run from −11 up through 14.
Stored as units (a sum over every house cell) and as four times that. Both are saved.
The governor's rank (1 for a new game) and the difficulty. The difficulty is the word the loader skips in the global block and keeps in the final state.
Peace, Culture, Prosperity, Empire, and their average.
Regular, irregular and auxiliary Centuries, this year and last.
The pleb count, its five duty assignments and the unassigned remainder, welfare, and the needs each duty has.

spec.title: What this can't tell you
spec.body: The middle of an actor record. A handful of the state bits in the part-index layer. The embedded province map holds scenario plus game state, and which of its changes are general rules rests on one scenario. And all seventeen real saves it was checked against are from one scenario (the embedded map is EMPIRE2.047) and from the first rank, so a field that only varies in another province or after a promotion could hide. The block layout comes from the executable's own writer and loader, not from those saves, which is why it can be stated as certain.

name: .VAS
title: The Caesar .VAS battle animation format
note: Frames of XOR deltas over a picture's four planes: the battle screen's win and loss animations. Played over WAR2.VPX, they draw the battle.
summary: The two animations on the battle screen, LOSE0001 and WINS0001, are not videos. Each frame is a list of byte runs to XOR onto the four planes of a .VPX picture, so the animation accumulates over whatever the screen already shows.

spec.title: Layout
body: The player loads the whole file and, for each frame in turn, reads that frame's 32-bit offset from a table near the start. For each of the four planes it selects the plane and XORs that plane's block onto the screen, stepping to the next block by the block's own length. Each frame is drawn onto both display pages.

spec.title: The file
spec.note: The rest of the first 0x14 bytes is not used by the player.

rows.name: frame count + 1
rows.description: One more than the number of frames.

rows.name: frame offsets
rows.description: One 32-bit offset per frame, into the file. LOSE0001.VAS has 21 frames, WINS0001.VAS 20.

spec.title: A frame: four plane blocks, back to back
spec.note: The plane is the same 16,000-byte quarter a .VPX block decodes to: pixel 4i + p is byte i of plane p.

rows.name: block length
rows.description: From the start of this block to the start of the next.

rows.name: plane size
rows.description: Always 16000.

rows.name: skipped
rows.description: The decoder steps over these.

rows.name: runs
rows.description: Each a word w. If bit 15 is set, XOR the next (w & 0x7FFF) + 1 bytes of the file onto the plane. Otherwise skip (w & 0x7FFF) + 1 bytes of the plane. Runs continue until their counts reach the plane size.

spec.title: What this can't tell you
spec.body: What the first 0x14 bytes beyond the frame count hold. One of the three players in the executable stops LOSE0001 after 13 frames; why is not established. Both files were checked by every block ending exactly where the next begins, and by playing them over WAR2.VPX in the WAR2 palette, which draws the battle.

name: CONTFRM.GD8 / EDATA.CSR
title: Caesar's screen data files: CONTFRM.GD8 and EDATA.CSR
note: Two small data files the screens read: the Forum picture's click map, and the province markers on the map of the Empire.
summary: The Forum is a painting with eight figures in it, each an advisor, and a click on a figure opens his screen. Which pixel belongs to which figure is not in the code; it is in a 1,000-byte file. The map of the Empire gets the position of each province's marker from a second one.

spec.title: CONTFRM.GD8, 1,000 bytes
spec.note: Loaded whole by the Forum screen. The shapes of the non-zero regions match the painted figures exactly.

rows.name: click map
rows.description: A grid of 40 columns by 25 rows, each cell covering 8 × 8 pixels of the 320 × 200 Forum picture (NEWFORUM.VPX). A cell is 0 or the number of a figure. The engine takes the cell under the mouse, (x / 8) + (y / 8) × 40, and a non-zero value v calls the far pointer at 4v in a table of eight handlers, one per advisor.

spec.title: EDATA.CSR, 320 bytes
spec.note: The values are byte-swapped relative to everything else in the game: stored big-endian, read as little-endian words and swapped.

rows.name: province markers
rows.description: For each of the 50 provinces, two big-endian words: x and y. The map draws a marker at x − 8, y − 32 (and 10 more in x for province 39).

rows.name: not read
rows.description: This build never loads them. What they were for is not known.

spec.title: What this can't tell you
spec.body: What the last 120 bytes of EDATA.CSR hold. The click map differs in the international build because its Forum picture does.

name: .VOC / .XMI / SAMPLE.AD
title: Caesar's sound files: .VOC, .XMI and SAMPLE.AD
note: Three published formats: Creative Voice files for the effects, Miles Extended MIDI for the tunes, and a Miles timbre library for the FM chip. The game uses Miles's own drivers, whose source is public.
summary: Caesar's sound is off the shelf. The effects are Creative Labs voice files, the tunes are Miles Sound System Extended MIDI, and the drivers that play them are byte-identical to the Audio Interface Library 2.14 release, whose source its author released as freeware. None of these formats had to be reverse engineered; what had to be worked out is which file plays when.

spec.title: What there is
body: The US build has 23 .VOC effects, 14 .XMI tunes with 14 matching .XM2 files, and one timbre library, SAMPLE.AD. Four loadable drivers (SBFM.ADV, ADLIB.ADV, SBDIG.ADV, PCSPKR.ADV) sit between them and the hardware.

items.description: Creative Voice Files, a published format. Every one is 8-bit unsigned mono PCM in sound blocks, at 8 kHz or 4 kHz. On a Sound Blaster the game halves every sample's distance from 128 before it plays one.

Miles Extended MIDI (an IFF FORM XDIR / CAT XMID container; delays are summed delay bytes, there is no running status, and note-ons carry their durations). They convert to Standard MIDI at 120 ticks a second, and all 14 do. These are what the AdLib and Sound Blaster FM chip play.
The same tunes arranged for the PC speaker: the executable gives every tune the extension .xm2 when the speaker is the sound device.

The Global Timbre Library for the Yamaha YM3812 (OPL2): a directory of 6-byte entries (patch, bank, 32-bit offset) ending at bank 0xFF, each timbre a 16-bit length and, for the YM3812, 12 bytes: transpose, then the modulator's AVEKM, KSLTL, AD, SR and waveform select, a feedback and connection byte, and the carrier's five. 162 timbres, all 14 bytes; bank 127 is the rhythm channel's, one timbre per key, with the note it plays in the transpose byte. Every timbre any tune asks for is in it.

Byte-identical to the Audio Interface Library 2.14 drivers of 14 November 1992. SBFM.ADV is its XMIDI driver for one YM3812. PCSPKR.ADV differs from the release (8,434 bytes against 8,377), an earlier or later version.

spec.title: Which tune plays when
spec.note: Nothing loops: every tune plays once. CZAR102.XMI is named nowhere in the US executable (inference: unused), and there is no CZARJIN3.

items.description: The title screen.
Entering the city after the start screen.
Drawing the Forum picture.
Each advisor's screen as it opens. CZARJIN5 is also the Options screen's.
Promotion.
The last promotion, to Caesar.
The arrest, when the governor has been dismissed too often.

spec.title: The effects
spec.note: Only one sound plays at a time: an effect stops the tune, and a tune stops the effect. ATTACK, CHARGE, FLANK and TORTOISE are named nowhere in the US executable (inference: unused, perhaps for Cohort 2).

items.description: A construction command chosen.
A building demolished, set alight, or a fire put out.
A fountain running dry.
An invader or a rioter appears; the battle message; a Cohort reaching an army.
A message; victory or defeat; the warning that the provinces need more workers.

items.term: MKT_THEA, COLISEUM, HORSES, HUBBUB, WORKSHOP, FOUNTAIN, MARCHROM, MARCHBAR
items.description: City sounds: a theatre, a coliseum, a hippodrome, a forum or a market, a workshop, a working fountain, Roman walkers and barbarians in view. They take turns on a 512-step cycle, and one plays only if its source is on screen.

spec.title: What this can't tell you
spec.body: These are US-build facts. The international build ships its music as .MDI files, which are re-orchestrations rather than conversions; their timing confirms the .XMI conversion. How the drivers translate a timbre to YM3812 register writes is in the public AIL source and not repeated here.

name: Caesar II media & disc formats
note: The save and text formats now have written specs on this site; the music (Miles XMIDI + OPL3), Smacker movies, and CD/ISO/BIN-CUE disc layouts are read and reimplemented by the port but not yet written up here as their own pages.

name: .SAV
title: The Caesar II savegame format
note: Not a container at all: roughly 430 named game-state fields written back to back in a fixed order, none of it compressed, followed by a fixed 4,000-byte history tail. Every field's name, size and position comes straight from the recovered save/load code.
summary: A Caesar II save is the plainest format in the whole series once you have the source: the recovered savegame() function writes about 430 registered fields in order, then appends a sibling file whole. Nothing is inferred from a hex dump — every offset below follows directly from the recovered table.

body: savegame() and loadgame() in the recovered source read and write two things, in sequence. First, a 500-slot table of registered game-state blocks — some a single byte, most a 4-byte counter, a handful multi-kilobyte arrays — terminated by the first zero-size entry, which the write loop treats as the end. Second, the complete contents of a sibling history.dat file, exactly 4,000 bytes, copied in with one read() and one write() and never touched by the entry table at all.

Of the 500 declared slots, 432 carry real data; the rest are zero-size padding the loop never reaches. Those 432 add up to exactly 221,745 bytes. Add the 4,000-byte history tail and every Caesar II save is 225,745 bytes — confirmed by the port's own round-trip tests against the real engine, not measured off a sample of files.

spec.title: The largest blocks, in file order
spec.note: Offsets are cumulative, exactly as the registration table declares them. Scalars in between are omitted here — roughly 380 of them, mostly 4-byte counters and rates named for what they track (denarii, population, ind_tax_rate…) — the full list is in loadsave.c, linked above.

rows.name: view state
rows.description: Map mode, overlay mode, zoom level (written twice), map scroll direction and position.

rows.name: army_list
rows.description: Every field army.

rows.name: citizen_list
rows.description: Every citizen record.

rows.name: unit_list
rows.description: Military units.

rows.name: figure_list
rows.description: Every animated figure on the map — walkers, soldiers, wildlife. The most heavily annotated struct in the reconstruction: every field is cross-referenced against the functions that read it.

rows.name: arrow_list
rows.description: Projectiles and thrown weapons in flight.

rows.name: army_routes
rows.description: Pathing state for field armies.

rows.name: city_map
rows.description: 80×80 tiles, 20 bytes each. Independently confirmed: entities.h's CITY_W × CITY_H × CITY_CELL_BYTES macros multiply to exactly this figure.

rows.name: region_map
rows.description: 60×60 tiles, 8 bytes each. Same cross-check as city_map.

rows.name: battle_map
rows.description: 52×52 tiles, 4 bytes each. Same cross-check again.

rows.name: industry
rows.description: Per-province industry state.

rows.name: empire_won
rows.description: Province conquest flags.

rows.name: history.dat tail
rows.description: The complete contents of the separate history.dat file, copied in unmodified — not part of the registered entry table, and always exactly 4,000 bytes.

spec.title: Every unknown gap is a real field, not padding
spec.body: Watcom C defaults to 1-byte struct packing, so there is no implicit alignment padding anywhere in these records — every gap the reconstruction hasn't named is a genuinely unrecovered field, marked by its own byte offset rather than left invisible. Several such gaps in figure_rec, unit_rec and citizen_rec were cross-checked against the separate Mac (PowerPC, CodeWarrior) build of the same source and confirmed genuinely unused there too — not just unread in the DOS decompilation.

spec.title: Not compressed, unlike Caesar III's
spec.body: Caesar III's savegame is a chunk list, most of it compressed with PKWARE DCL. Caesar II's is not — every field above is written with a plain write() call, in the clear. The older game turns out to have the more transparent format.

name: .ENG / .HELP
title: Caesar II's text and help files
note: The addressing model and both files' buffer limits are confirmed from a byte-exact reimplementation; the on-disk group/page directory layout itself is not restated on this site.
summary: C2.ENG and HELP.ENG aren't text files in the ordinary sense. Every string is addressed by a (group, index) pair the game's own code compiles into, and a from-scratch reimplementation reproduces both files byte-for-byte in every language tested — which is why the model below can be stated as fact rather than read off a hex dump.

body: C2.ENG holds every string in the game — menus, panels, in-game messages — addressed as (group, index): a call site reads as font_list(0x2f, 3, …) to mean "string 3 of group 0x2f", and there are 147 groups. HELP.ENG is addressed differently, by help page number, and each page carries a title string and a body string plus non-text fields — an illustration name, a voice-clip name, a sprite id, layout widths — that the port treats as language-neutral and compiles from the 1996 English file regardless of which language's text is active.

Both files are read into fixed buffers the engine never grows: a help page into 2,000 bytes, the whole of C2.ENG into 40,000. A translation that overflows either limit is rejected before it ships, not discovered by a player.

items.description: 147 groups; two of them, 117 and 118, deliberately share group 116's payload, and 120 shares 119's — the same string reused under more than one address rather than duplicated.

Slot 0 is a page's title, slot 1 its body. A page that reuses another page's text stores the reference "@1234" instead of repeating it — the German translation uses this to link spare pages differently where a chapter ran long.
"$" is the engine's own line break; "#12text#" is a clickable link to help page 12, and both must survive translation unchanged.

spec.title: A shipped content bug, not a rendering bug
spec.body: The full English HELP.ENG contains four 0x92 bytes inside contractions and possessives. In Windows-1252 that byte is a curly right-quote; in Caesar II's own bitmap font table the same slot draws the DOS Æ glyph. The English 1995 demo omits the affected pages, but the retail and rerelease help files ship all four — every font asset examined across the DOS retail, Win95 rerelease and Mac demo agrees, so the visible Æ is a genuine authoring defect from 1995/96, not something a host text encoding could ever have fixed.

spec.title: Real translation bugs the tooling now corrects
spec.body: The 1995 French C2.ENG splits several strings with a NUL byte instead of a space and merges two others, which shifted every later index in four groups onto the wrong text in the shipped game; the 1995 releases also have no battle icon tooltips at all, so those groups alias a Senate letter instead. Both are documented, sourced defects in the original release — reproduced faithfully by a byte-exact reimplementation, and separately corrected in the reimplementation's own translation template with the reason recorded alongside the fix.
